record.paper_title: Retrieving Convex Bodies from Restricted Covariogram Functions
record.original_question: For a convex body, does the distribution of the lengths of its chords, taken in all directions, characterize the body up to rigid motions?

evidence.quote: Blaschke (cf. [San04]) asked whether the distribution of the lengths of chords (in all directions) of a convex body characterizes the body, up to rigid motions, but Mallows and Clark [MC70] proved that this is false even for convex polygons.

artifact.self_contained_problem: Let $K \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a convex body (i.e., a compact convex set with nonempty interior). For each unit direction $u \in S^{n-1}$ and each line $\ell$ parallel to $u$ meeting $K$, the intersection $\ell \cap K$ is a (possibly degenerate) line segment, called a chord of $K$. Considering all chords of $K$ in all directions (with the natural measure induced by, say, the product of Lebesgue measure on the space of lines and orientation), one obtains the chord-length distribution of $K$: the probability distribution of the lengths $|\ell \cap K|$.\n\nQuestion: Does the chord-length distribution of a convex body $K$ determine $K$ uniquely up to rigid motions of $\mathbb{R}^n$? That is, if two convex bodies $K_1, K_2 \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ have the same chord-length distribution, must there exist a rigid motion $T$ with $T(K_1) = K_2$?
artifact.status_search_result: The problem, originally posed by Blaschke, was resolved in the negative by Mallows and Clark (1970), who exhibited noncongruent convex polygons with the same chord-length distribution. Thus the chord-length distribution does not characterize a convex body up to rigid motions, even within the class of convex polygons.

status_evidence.title: Mallows–Clark, Linear-intercept distributions do not characterize plane sets
status_evidence.snippet: Mallows and Clark (1970) showed that the distribution of chord lengths does not characterize a convex polygon up to congruence, giving an explicit counterexample.
status_evidence.claim: Blaschke's question has a negative answer, established by Mallows and Clark in 1970.
